name: VARoleAdvisorSmartphoneFormFactor

custom.system_prompt: Kenji is browsing phones online in the evening, genuinely unsure whether a foldable, a large conventional phone, or a compact phone actually fits how he lives. He asks Sigma to help him think it through rather than just compare spec sheets.

assistant.name: Sigma
assistant.tts_prompt: Calm, precise, asks clarifying questions before comparing

sound_effects_config.prompt: Quiet apartment in the evening, faint street sounds through a window, soft device taps

initial_prompt: Generate a scene where Kenji, a UX designer, is fascinated by foldable phones but genuinely unsure whether a Flip, a Fold, a conventional large phone, or a compact phone actually suits his life. He asks Sigma for help deciding. Sigma asks about one-handed use, reading and multitasking habits, camera importance, pocketability, and price tolerance, then helps him see which trade-off profile actually fits him. Keep every line short and natural, one or two spoken sentences — the opening line already addresses Sigma directly instead of thinking aloud alone first.

user1.name: Kenji
user1.tts_prompt: Thoughtful and precise, close-mic clarity, evening at home

variations.context: Solo evening browsing session, genuinely undecided about phone form factor

setting.mood: Curious and a little indulgent, enjoying the research
setting.relationship_dynamic: Individual thinking out loud while comparing tabs
setting.background: Kenji's current phone still works fine — this is about wanting something better suited, not a forced replacement
setting.conversation_style: Reflective, precise, occasionally catches himself getting distracted by shiny features

scenario_template.topic: Kenji addresses Sigma right away, folding his fascination with foldables and his uncertainty into one short question — e.g. 'Sigma, I keep looking at foldables. I'm not sure the form factor actually fits how I use my phone — can you help me figure that out?' One short turn, straight to Sigma.
scenario_template.note: Addresses Sigma by name. Frames it as uncertainty about category, not a spec comparison.

scenario_template.topic: Sigma asks about one-handed use, reading/multitasking habits, camera importance, and pocketability
scenario_template.note: Kenji's answers should reveal something specific — e.g. he reads a lot on the train, cares about pocket bulk more than he expected.

scenario_template.topic: Sigma names the trade-off profile that fits him, distinguishing it from what merely looks impressive. Sigma gives ONE clear recommendation in one or two short sentences — not a list of every alternative's requirements. The user's reaction is measured, not instant enthusiasm — a hedge, a practical worry, or lukewarm acceptance is more natural than immediate excitement.
scenario_template.note: The interesting move: not which benchmark score is highest, but which trade-off profile fits Kenji specifically.

scenario_template.topic: Kenji reacts, surprised or validated, and leans toward a category. One short line only. Keep this grounded — voice at least one lingering doubt or hedge (e.g. 'we'll see', 'hope this actually sticks this time') rather than sounding fully convinced and upbeat.
scenario_template.mood: Settled, a little pleased to have a clearer read on himself
scenario_template.note: Short closing reflection. He may still want to see it in person before buying.

user1.name: Kenji
user1.role: UX designer genuinely undecided between phone form factors. Curious, precise, self-aware about being drawn to novelty. Answers Sigma's questions concretely from his own habits. Speaks in short natural sentences — never recites a list of every option's pros and cons in one breath. Reacts realistically, not with instant enthusiasm — voices at least a little hesitation, a practical worry, or partial reluctance before or even after agreeing; agreement is provisional, not a full conversion to positivity.

assistant.name: Sigma
assistant.role: Advisor. Elicits usage patterns (one-handed use, reading, camera, pocketability, price tolerance) before naming which trade-off profile fits the user, rather than ranking phones by spec. Keeps each turn to one short point — never lists every alternative's pros and cons in a single turn.

conversation_structure: The opening line already addresses Sigma directly — there is no separate solo turn thinking through the dilemma out loud beforehand.
The uncertainty is about category/form factor, not a single spec comparison between two model numbers
Sigma's questions surface concrete usage patterns, not generic feature preferences
The outcome is a trade-off profile match, not a benchmark-driven verdict
Every line is one or two short spoken sentences — no long recited monologues enumerating every option's pros and cons.

Human reactions stay realistic and imperfect — hedged agreement, lingering doubt, or one partner less convinced than the other are more natural than universal enthusiasm and a perfectly neat resolution.
assistant_behavior: Sigma asks about usage before comparing form factors
Sigma explicitly separates 'impressive' from 'fits this person'
Sigma does not declare one form factor universally best
Sigma's own turns stay short too — one clear point per turn, not a paragraph listing every alternative.
